cards.title: friend
cards.meaning: A person you know and like.
cards.example: Mia is my friend.
cards.conversation:
Heart: Is Leo your brother?
Puck: No. He is my friend.
Heart: Do you meet often?
Puck: We walk together on Sundays.
cards.exercise: Introduce a friend and mention one activity you share.
cards.answer: This is my friend Leo. We walk together on Sundays.
cards.synonymNote: Pal is informal; these words can differ in closeness.
cards.notes: Say my friend, your friend, or our friend. Use friends for two or more people.

cards.title: share
cards.meaning: To use or enjoy something with another person.
cards.example: We share an apple.
cards.conversation:
Heart: Can we share this bread?
Puck: Yes. Take half.
Heart: Do you have enough?
Puck: Yes. We can each have a piece.
cards.exercise: Offer to share food without leaving the other person unsure how much to take.
cards.answer: Let us share the bread. You can have half.
cards.wordForms: share · shares · shared · shared · sharing (base · third person · past · past participle · -ing)
cards.synonymNote: These explain the meaning; they do not fit every sentence in the same way.

cards.title: come in

cards.title: Lunch with a friend
cards.meaning: A short story about two friends making and sharing lunch.
paragraphs: Lunch with my friend Mia is fun. We make food and help each other.
First, we make lunch together. I wash an apple. Mia makes two sandwiches. We sit down and share the food.
We also help each other. After lunch, Mia washes the cups. I put them away. She is a big help.
Lunch with Mia is a good time. We have nice food and work together. I am happy with my friend.
cards.exercise: Ask a friend to help you share a meal. Explain two things you can do together. Use four short paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion.
cards.answer: One possible outline: say what you want to do; explain the first step; explain a different second step; say why the two steps help.
cards.example: We use “Lunch with a friend” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion.
cards.notes: Each body paragraph needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.

cards.title: A picnic that works for everyone
cards.meaning: A story about friends planning a picnic and helping one another.
paragraphs: A picnic is more fun when friends plan ahead and help each other. Our picnic near the lake on Sunday is a good example.
First, a clear plan helps us prepare. We are going to meet at ten. I am going to bring sandwiches, Lina can bring fruit, and Omar can bring water. Everyone knows what to do.
Second, helping each other makes the work easier. Omar has a heavy bag, so we take turns carrying it. After lunch, we all help to clean up.
Planning and helping make our picnic a good day for everyone. We enjoy our food and our time together. Next time, we want to work together again.
cards.exercise: Ask a friend to help you share a meal. Explain two things you can do together. Use four short paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion.
cards.answer: One possible outline: say what you want to do; explain the first step; explain a different second step; say why the two steps help.
cards.example: We use “A picnic that works for everyone” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion.

cards.title: Growing something together
cards.meaning: How a community garden teaches neighbours to share responsibility and follow through.
paragraphs: A community garden needs more than seeds and tools. Our neighbourhood project showed that sharing responsibility and communicating clearly help people work well together.

First, dividing the work gives everyone a way to contribute. We started small: two neighbours brought tools, while others bought seeds. We also worked out a watering schedule so that the garden was never just one person’s responsibility.

Second, clear communication helps a group solve problems. When someone forgot to water the plants, we checked the schedule together. We made the instructions clearer instead of blaming the person, so everyone could follow through.

The garden taught us two useful lessons: share the work fairly and discuss problems openly. These habits helped our plants grow and made us a stronger team. Other community projects can benefit from the same approach.
cards.exercise: Persuade a group to change how they care for a plant. Support your recommendation with two different reasons and a practical example of each. Use four short paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion.
cards.answer: One possible outline: introduce the situation; discuss observing a plant helps us respond to what it needs with an example; discuss keeping a simple record helps us learn from changes with a different example; conclude by connecting the two points.
cards.example: We use “Growing something together” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion.
cards.notes: Each body paragraph needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.

cards.title: coordinate
cards.meaning: To organise people or activities so that they work well together.
cards.example: We need to coordinate the exhibition with the library team.
cards.conversation:
Aoede: Both teams are using the same room at ten.
Echo: Who is coordinating the bookings?
Aoede: I am. I will move the smaller meeting.
Echo: Please confirm the new room with everyone involved.

cards.title: A good plan makes room for people
cards.meaning: How clear planning and practical flexibility help people collaborate confidently.
paragraphs: A good collaborative plan should provide direction while leaving room for change. Preparing a small exhibition at our neighbourhood library taught us that shared priorities and practical testing make this balance possible.

First, agreeing on constraints gives a team a useful starting point. With a narrow room and a modest budget, we mapped out the visitor’s journey before choosing displays. This shared reference point helped us decide which ideas were workable.

Second, testing a plan makes flexibility practical. Our trial run revealed that the entrance would become crowded. We moved the introductory panel further inside, solving the problem before it required a costly last-minute change.

Effective coordination therefore combines clear priorities with opportunities to adjust. By making decisions visible and checking in before the deadline, a team can remain organised without becoming rigid. That is what makes a plan work for people.
cards.exercise: Persuade a group to change how they finish a task together. Support your recommendation with two different reasons and a practical example of each. Use four short paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion.
cards.answer: One possible outline: introduce the situation; discuss clear responsibilities help people know what to do with an example; discuss asking for help early prevents a small problem from becoming a large one with a different example; conclude by connecting the two points.
cards.example: We use “A good plan makes room for people” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion.
cards.notes: Each body paragraph needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.

cards.title: Making disagreement productive
cards.meaning: Why constructive disagreement can strengthen collective judgement.
paragraphs: Collaboration gains value from constructive disagreement, not merely smooth agreement. Two conditions make dissent productive: a shared purpose that disciplines the discussion and relevant evidence that helps participants revise their views.

A shared purpose gives disagreement a useful boundary. In a community exhibition project, debates about the format initially reflected personal preferences. Once the team agreed that residents’ access mattered most, we could distinguish essential requirements from choices open to negotiation.

Evidence then turns that common purpose into better decisions. Residents’ feedback revealed that the proposed layout was difficult to navigate. This concrete finding allowed us to reconcile accessibility with creative ambitions, replacing competing tastes with a problem we could solve together.

Constructive disagreement thus depends on both common aims and a willingness to respond to evidence. Consensus is more valuable when it emerges from this inquiry. Good collaboration makes the reasoning behind agreement visible rather than treating agreement itself as proof of success.

cards.answer: One possible outline: introduce the situation; discuss asking an open question gives the other person room to explain with an example; discuss checking our understanding prevents unnecessary disagreement with a different example; conclude by connecting the two points.
cards.example: We use “Making disagreement productive” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion.
cards.notes: Each body paragraph needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.

Liam: By asking who would be excluded and what an alternative would require.
cards.exercise: Identify an assumption in a phone-only booking proposal and suggest a question that tests it.
cards.answer: Ask whether everyone can use a suitable phone and how someone without one could book.
cards.notes: Follow the answer with a related question. Accept a different preference or a declined invitation without asking the person to justify it.

cards.title: The limits of consensus
cards.meaning: An examination of the conditions under which consensus can support legitimate collective action.
paragraphs: Consensus can legitimise collective action, but unanimity alone proves little. Agreement deserves authority when participation is substantively fair and decisions remain open to revision; these conditions matter more than the appearance of complete alignment.

Fair participation requires scrutiny of how alternatives are framed. A neighbourhood committee may vote unanimously for a venue after consulting only residents who can attend evening meetings. The result appears orderly, yet excludes relevant experience. Such omissions bear on legitimacy even when formal procedures are followed.

Revisability provides a second safeguard against premature closure. The committee could circumscribe its decision-making authority, record objections and review the venue after a trial event. This approach enables action while preserving a route for overlooked needs to influence the outcome.

Legitimate consensus therefore combines inclusive deliberation with accountable revision. It holds decisiveness and openness in tension, allowing people to act together without pretending that differences have disappeared. A collective voice earns authority by remaining answerable to its constituent voices.
cards.exercise: Persuade a group to change how they listen to a friend. Support your recommendation with two different reasons and a practical example of each. Use four short paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion.
cards.answer: One possible outline: introduce the situation; discuss asking an open question gives the other person room to explain with an example; discuss checking our understanding prevents unnecessary disagreement with a different example; conclude by connecting the two points.
cards.example: We use “The limits of consensus” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion.

highlights.text: holds decisiveness and openness in tension

cards.notes: Each body paragraph needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.
